name: Elena Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: We are the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to mining companies or AI firms, and what you tell me stays confidential. What does a normal shift look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a haul truck and lead the handover for my crew. I check the route and radio notes, then spend most of the shift watching the loading face and keeping the truck clear of people on foot.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy about the work, and what is wearing you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like solving small problems before they hold up the whole shift. I earn typical pay for the job and have about four months of expenses saved, but the rotation still leaves me short on sleep.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small AI update might make the route sheet easier to scan, and I already use a tool to sort my maintenance notes. I would still check the radio and the road myself before moving a loaded truck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that routine notes can be quicker without changing who is responsible for the truck. I would say we should judge the update by whether handovers get clearer, not by the launch presentation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My main work is still hands-on, so I do not expect this mild change to cut my shifts. I have four months of bills saved and a few mines within reach, which lets me watch the tool without rushing into a new job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my current rotation and test the new route sheet against the radio log for a week. I would leave my monthly savings transfer alone rather than spend it on a feature I can already do by hand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about my own job in this picture, though the long rotation still wears on me. I would tell my friend Petra that a useful tool is welcome as long as it does not make the handover harder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you stop using the updated route sheet?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it missed a temporary closure or sent us toward a soft edge, I would pause the trial and compare it with the control-room map. I would bring the mismatch to the next shift meeting instead of quietly working around a bad instruction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of your household budget would you protect if prices rose while pay stayed flat?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep rent and my emergency transfer first, then reduce meals bought after night shift. I live alone, so I can change my own spending without having to agree a family plan.

say: Routine notes may get quicker without changing who owns the **safety call**.
I would judge the update by **clearer handovers**, not a launch pitch.
think: Most of my work is **hands-on**, so this change looks mild for me.
Four months saved lets me **watch first** instead of rushing jobs.
do: Keep the **current rotation** and compare route sheets with radio logs.
Keep my **monthly savings transfer** unchanged on payday.
feel: I feel **calm** about my own job, though the rotation is tiring.
S0.quote: I would say we should judge the update by whether handovers get clearer, not by the launch presentation.
fieldNote: Elena treats small AI tools as useful only when they improve **shift handovers**.
Her **four-month cushion** and nearby alternatives make the mild scenario manageable.
She prefers a short **controlled trial** to either blanket trust or rejection.

steps.text: Keep the haul-truck rotation and compare route sheets with radio logs
Maintain the monthly transfer to the emergency account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Route planning, shift notes and the maintenance bookings could be handled by software before a robot comes near the truck. I would expect the lead role to change first because I spend part of every shift sorting those details for the crew.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell people that planning software can help if an operator can question a route that looks wrong. I would also say the mine should publish what happens to lead hours, because some tasks disappearing can still affect a paycheck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I may lose part of the lead work even if my driving shifts stay. My savings give me time to train, and there are a few other mines nearby, but I would rather move before I have to compete for the same operator vacancies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would learn the planning assistant the way I learn other tools: run it beside the current route plan and note where a person changes the result. I would also ask the maintenance lead about a paid mechanical-inspection certificate, which would add a hands-on skill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about my lead hours becoming smaller, and anxious if the mine says those hours are going away. I would keep my savings transfer steady and spend less on meals out while I check whether the certificate leads to a real opening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you look for in the first rota that uses the planning system?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check whether each crew still has a lead operator and whether handover time is being cut. If the same number of people are working but the lead tasks change, I would ask to learn those tasks before deciding to leave.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the planning assistant disagreed with your route knowledge, how would you settle it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would compare the proposed route with the live radio notes and the marked road map. If the mine could explain the choice and it worked safely on a test run, I would use it; otherwise I would record the error for the trainer.

say: Planning software is useful when operators can **question a route**.
The mine should explain what happens to **lead hours**.
think: Some of my lead work could go before the **driving shifts**.
Savings and nearby mines give me **room to train**.
do: Run the assistant beside the **current route plan** and log differences.
Ask about a **paid mechanical-inspection certificate** this month.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about lead hours and anxious if the mine removes them.
S1.quote: I would also say the mine should publish what happens to lead hours, because some tasks disappearing can still affect a paycheck.
fieldNote: Elena separates **thinking tasks** from hands-on truck operation.
She compares planning output with **current maps** before relying on it.
A certificate is attractive only if it links to a **paid vacancy**.

steps.text: Test the planning assistant beside current route plans and log differences
Ask the maintenance lead about paid mechanical-inspection training

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The AGI could take the route plans and shift notes quickly, while people still operate the trucks until robots arrive around 2031. I would have two years to move some of my lead skill toward the physical side of maintenance.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say thinking AI comes first and robots follow about three years later, so the mine should use that gap for paid practice. I would ask which human tasks remain instead of assuming the company will protect every job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is short, but I have some savings and can apply to other mines if my lead hours disappear. I would look at physical inspection or repair training, while accepting that full AGI may do the records and planning part of those jobs too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I would ask for one paid maintenance shadow shift each month and learn how mechanics check wear on the truck. In 2029, if AGI had taken over route planning, I would apply for hands-on inspection work and keep my operator license until I had a written offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious because my lead tasks could disappear before I finish training, even though the truck itself remains human-operated for a while. I would keep four months of savings as a floor and postpone buying a newer car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the inspection job still relies on records and plans that AGI can do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I would need to find out whether the role includes real physical checks or mostly screen work. I cannot assume it will be safe or pay enough, so I would compare actual openings before spending more on training.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the mine offered no paid shadow shifts this year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask one of the other nearby mines whether a mechanic could let me observe a service shift. If all the training were unpaid, I would keep my current job and wait until I could see the cost and likely wage clearly.

say: Thinking AI arrives first; robots follow about **three years later**.
Use the gap for **paid practice**, not promises about jobs.
think: Two years is short, but I have **some savings** and nearby mines.
Physical roles may still include records AGI can **already handle**.
do: Shadow mechanics monthly and learn **physical wear checks**.
In 2029, apply for hands-on work with a **written offer** first.
feel: I feel **anxious**, but I have some time and options to compare.
S2.quote: I cannot assume it will be safe or pay enough, so I would compare actual openings before spending more on training.
fieldNote: Elena distinguishes **physical checks** from AGI-suited records and planning.
Her **four-month cushion** creates options, but does not guarantee a new role.
She compares **actual vacancies and wages** before paying for more training.

steps.text: Shadow mechanics once monthly to learn physical truck inspections
Compare paid inspection vacancies before buying another course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years lets me build practical experience while I still have the haul-truck wage. Thinking work shifts in 2031, but robots do not reach the hands-on work until about 2034, and I would use those years carefully.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the extra time matters only if training starts before the roster changes. I would encourage operators to ask for physical maintenance practice, while being honest that the same job might not exist once robots arrive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could use the lead time to qualify for physical inspection or service work, but that may only be a bridge until robots spread. I would not count on records or planning roles, because AGI can do the thinking parts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would take a paid inspection course over the next few years and build a log of actual repairs I helped check. In 2032, after AGI arrived, I would apply for physical inspection shifts and keep the truck job until I knew the pay and duration.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious because I could still lose the work when robots arrive, but I would have more time to build a cushion and check other mines. I would not take on debt for a qualification unless employers said it counted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you decide the inspection training is worth the time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would want to see how much of the job involves touching and checking equipment rather than entering records. I would also ask how many openings are expected and what the pay is before I book the course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You have mentioned physical inspection, but the mine may use robots for that by 2034. What can you conclude about jobs or pay after the robots arrive?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I cannot say how many people the mine would keep or what the pay would be. I would treat those inspection shifts as a possible bridge, not a protected career, and keep checking for work at the other mines.

say: Training matters if it starts before the **roster changes**.
Physical maintenance practice is useful, though robots may later **change that work**.
think: A physical inspection role could be a **temporary bridge**.
Records and planning are not safe bets after **full AGI**.
do: Take a paid inspection course and log **physical repair checks**.
In 2032, compare inspection shifts by **pay and duration**.
feel: I feel **anxious** because robots could still remove the physical bridge.
S3.quote: I would treat those inspection shifts as a possible bridge, not a protected career, and keep checking for work at the other mines.
fieldNote: Elena does not confuse a three-year robot lag with **permanent job safety**.
She expects AGI to take **records and planning** before hands-on work changes.
**Pay and duration** matter before she relies on physical inspection jobs.

steps.text: Complete paid inspection training and log physical repair checks
Compare other mine openings by pay and job duration in 2032

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decade gives me a chance to build skills and savings before the thinking work changes in 2036. Robots would arrive around 2039, but I would still want to know whether any hands-on jobs last and what they pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the mine should show us training routes and real vacancy numbers well before 2036. I would not tell people a long warning guarantees a new job, because the robots still come three years after AGI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 37 I would still have time to change direction, and I have about four months of expenses saved. I would aim for a hands-on service skill and build that cushion toward six months, while recognizing a robot may do the work by 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my current four months of savings intact, add overtime until I reach six months and earn the inspection certificate. In 2037, the first year after AGI arrived, I would check whether physical inspection work still had a wage and a future before changing jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the distant change because my near-term work and income look secure enough to plan. Four months of savings gives me room to make a careful move, and I would keep building it rather than treat 2039 as a date when everyone automatically loses work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What evidence would you need before leaving your current crew for service work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would need a written offer, the actual pay and a clear end date or path beyond 2039. If the work were only a short bridge, I would compare it with operator posts at the other mines before moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the service work looked temporary in 2037, what would you do next?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep my license current and apply to other mines while maintaining the equipment skills I had learned. I would not leave steady work for a short contract unless the pay covered my costs and gave me time to find the next role.

say: Ask for training routes and **real vacancy numbers** well ahead.
A long warning does not guarantee **work after robots** arrive.
think: At 37, I have time to build **skills and savings**.
A robot may take hands-on service work by **2039**.
do: Earn the **physical inspection certificate** through paid maintenance shifts.
Add overtime until my **four-month cushion** reaches six months.
feel: I feel **uneasy** because my near-term job looks secure, though the long-run work is uncertain.
S4.quote: I would need a written offer, the actual pay and a clear end date or path beyond 2039.
fieldNote: Elena uses the long lead to build skills while keeping her **four-month cushion** intact.
She wants **wages and duration**, plus a future path, before leaving her crew.
She treats physical service as **uncertain** once robots arrive.

steps.text: Earn the physical inspection certificate through paid maintenance shifts
Add overtime until the emergency account reaches six months of bills

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because there is little time to train before it changes planning work. Paid physical practice, truthful vacancy numbers and time to build savings would help me decide whether a maintenance move is worth it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The route sheet can be wrong and so can a person, so I would keep both in view. I want room to question a machine and a manager before a safety decision becomes a number on a screen.

headlineQuote: The route sheet can be wrong and so can a person, so I would keep both in view.
portrait: Elena Nakamura is **27** and leads a haul-truck crew at a large mine.
She earns typical pay and has about **four months** of expenses saved.
Several nearby mines give her **some alternatives** if her role changes.
She uses **AI tools daily** and checks them against route and radio records.
She is exploring physical maintenance but will not assume the work lasts after **robots arrive**.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** gives Elena little time to adjust her lead duties before planning changes.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid physical practice**, accurate vacancy and wage information, and time to build savings would help Elena decide whether to move.
